QF.id: SIA Social Stock Exchange Introduction and Instruments_37

question.text: The Indian SSE differs from pure 'matchmaking platform' models (e.g., Brazil's BVSA or South Africa's SASIX) because:

answer.text: It excludes NPOs entirely and serves only FPEs.

It will allow trading for equities issued by FPEs, direct listing for NPOs, a full range of standardised funding mechanisms, a reporting standard, and incentives to attract investors — i.e., it is both a place and a set of processes.
It operates exclusively as a donor-NPO directory with no listing or trading function.
It is a pay-to-list platform where both NPOs and FPEs pay annual listing fees of Rs 1 crore.

explanation.text: The Logic: Per Section 2.1 (Box 2.1), 'By contrast, the Indian SSE will allow trading for equities issued by FPEs, and for NPOs, the SSE will open up avenues for direct listing, will streamline a whole range of funding mechanisms, and will provide a reporting standard and other incentives that will pull investors onto it.' The SSE 'is a set of processes as much as it is a place'. The Trap: Option A is wrong — NPOs are core constituents. Option C reduces the SSE to a directory (matchmaking model). Option D invents a fee structure. Cross-Exam Context: XII (SMF) treats the global taxonomy of exchanges — cash, segmented, matchmaking. V-B (MF Foundation) references the 'platform vs process' dichotomy. Assessor's Pro-Tip: When benchmarking your NPO client's reporting against global standards, avoid using BVSA or SASIX as comparators — their NPOs don't follow the same Annual-Impact-Report discipline; use India-listed peers on NSE-SSE or BSE-SSE for like-for-like comparability.
